This integration brings a **NASweb module** (nasWebio, Chomtech) into Gladys,
on your local network, without any cloud: its **relay outputs**, its
**inputs** and its **temperature probe**.

Unofficial integration, not affiliated with nasWebio. **Never tested with a
real module**: it follows the local API used by the manufacturer's own
library (webio-api, the one of Home Assistant's NASweb integration). Please
report on the Gladys forum whether it works with yours.

## What you get

| On the module              | In Gladys                                                                |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Relay output declared safe | A switch (on / off), only if you allow the commands                      |
| Other relay output         | Its state, read only (no command at all)                                 |
| Input                      | "Input active" (1 active, 0 normal) and "Input fault or tamper" (1 or 0) |
| Temperature probe          | Temperature in °C, once the module reported a value                      |

The outputs and inputs appear in the **Discovery** tab once the module has
sent its first status. Alarm zones and the thermostat of the module are not
offered (they arm, disarm or heat: out of scope for this first version).
The module API gives no humidity value: none is offered.

## How the states arrive

The module **pushes** its states: it posts them to an address it was given
(a "status subscription"). The integration container cannot receive
anything from the network, so Gladys starts a small **receiver** next to it
(the `nasweb-push` container, same image) and publishes one port for it,
chosen by Gladys. The receiver starts, and its port exists, only once the
address of the module, the login and the password are saved: until then the
configuration screen shows `{{port:nasweb_push}}` as is; save first, then
reload the screen. The integration subscribes the module itself to
`http://<address of Gladys>:<that port>/nasweb/<secret>`:

- the secret part is random, generated once for your installation, kept in
  the Gladys configuration (never shown), and never written to the logs. It
  travels **in clear** (HTTP, the module posts no other way) at every post:
  whoever can see this traffic on your network (open Wi-Fi, port mirroring,
  ARP spoofing) can read it and post;
- the receiver accepts exactly that address and the POST method, 32 KB at
  most. With the sender checked, the module may post 240 times a minute and
  any other sender is refused (403); otherwise each sender may post 60 times
  a minute (240 in all), and beyond that its latest post is kept and sent
  once its minute frees. 32 connections at most, 4 per sender, 4 kept for
  the module: over a limit, the oldest connection whose request is not
  complete is closed (one that sent nothing first), not the new one. A connection that sends nothing is closed
  within 10 s (about 5 s), and a request must arrive whole within about
  11 s; everything else is refused;
- with **Check the sender of the states** (on by default), only the address
  of the module may post: the receiver refuses the others before anything
  else, and the integration checks again;
- the integration then accepts a status only if it carries the **serial
  number** of the module. That number is no secret (it is shown in the
  status and in the NASWEB_SERIAL parameter): it only tells another module
  apart, not an attacker.

If Docker hides the real address of the sender on your machine (every
status then seems to come from an address like 172.x.x.1, and the status
says so), you may turn off "Check the sender of the states". Know what it
lets through: anyone who has read the secret address can then post forged
states (relays, inputs, temperature), and so start your scenes.

There is no other way to read the states: if no status arrives for 90
seconds, the devices are shown **unreachable**, the module is read again
(identity, subscription) at most once a minute, and the subscription is
renewed every 10 minutes.

## Configuration

1. Give the module a **fixed IP address** in your router.
2. In Gladys, Integrations → NASweb → Configuration:
   - **Address of the module**: its IP address (the one of its web page),
     optionally with its HTTPS port, for example `192.168.1.50`;
   - **Login** and **Password** of the web page of the module. The password
     is kept by Gladys in its database, never shown again, and only sent to
     the module, as the module expects it (a SHA-1 hash, which is as good as
     the password for the module: treat it as such);
   - **Address of Gladys**: the IP address of the machine running Gladys, as
     the module reaches it, for example `192.168.1.10` (no port);
   - save.
3. If your Gladys machine has a firewall, allow the port shown in the
   configuration screen (receiver block).
4. The status says "Connected" once the first status arrived. The outputs
   and inputs are then in the Discovery tab.

### Relay outputs: switches only when declared safe

A relay may drive a lamp, but also a pump, a boiler, a heater or a gate. A
switch is reached by "turn everything off" of voice assistants, of scenes
and of the dashboard. So:

- only the outputs listed in **Outputs declared safe** (their numbers, the
  NASWEB_OUTPUT parameter of the Discovery tab, for example `1, 2, 5`)
  become switches; list only loads that may be switched off or on at any
  time;
- every other output is its **state, read only**: no command can reach it
  from Gladys;
- **Allow the commands** is off by default: until you turn it on, every
  command is refused, even on a switch.

An output removed from the list keeps the switch already created in Gladys
(its history is kept), but every command on it is refused.

### When a command is accepted

A command on a switch is refused (nothing sent to the module) when:

- "Allow the commands" is off, or the output is not declared safe;
- the value is not exactly on (1) or off (0);
- the module was never identified, or no longer reports this output;
- the last status of the module was posted more than 90 seconds ago (the
  result could not be confirmed);
- the module refused the login, its certificate changed, or another serial
  number answers at its address;
- the saved state of the integration (`/data`) cannot be read;
- the module does not answer, or answers with an error, while its identity
  is read again;
- the configuration changed during the command;
- the module answers too slowly: the identity read and the command must
  leave within 3.5 seconds of the click (a command on the same output first
  waits for the write of the previous one).

Before each command the integration reads the identity of the module again
(its serial number). Once the command has left, the answer is one of:

- success: a status posted after the write shows the requested state,
  within about 4 seconds of the click;
- "Sent, without confirmation": no such status in time, no answer from the
  module, an error answer (HTTP code) or an unreadable one;
- "the module answered that the command failed" (its answer is not "OK");
- "the module refused the command (login refused)": the integration then
  stops, as for a refused login;
- "replaced by a newer command": another command on the same output left
  before this one was confirmed.

## Security

- The module serves a self-signed certificate. Its fingerprint is **pinned**
  at the first connection (kept in `/data` before the login ever leaves);
  another certificate is refused before anything is sent. If you replaced or
  updated the module, the status shows the new fingerprint: press **Trust
  the device now answering** twice within 60 seconds (the first press only
  shows what answers). The same button accepts a new serial number (a
  replaced module: its outputs become new devices).
- A refused login stops everything, even after a restart: correct the
  credentials and save, or press **Test the connection**. The integration
  never retries by itself.
- No credential, secret address or token is ever written to the logs, to
  `/data` or to the status.

## Buttons

- **Test the connection**: reads the module now with the saved
  configuration (even after a refused login), subscribes it to the states,
  and says what answered. At most every 10 seconds.
- **Trust the device now answering**: see Security.

## Troubleshooting

- _"waiting for its first status"_: the module does not reach Gladys. Check
  the address of Gladys, the firewall of the Gladys machine, and that the
  module and Gladys are on the same network (or routed). Browsing Gladys
  through Gladys Plus or a reverse proxy does not change anything: the
  module must reach the LAN address of the Gladys machine.
- _"status(es) refused: they came from 172…"_: see "How the states arrive".
- _"Module unreachable"_: check the address of the module and that its web
  page opens.

## Configuration settings

These are the settings NASweb asks for in its configuration screen in Gladys.

| Setting | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Your NASweb module, on your local network | `section` | No | Relay outputs, inputs and the temperature probe of a NASweb module, through its local API, without any cloud. The module sends its states to Gladys by itself (a small receiver started by Gladys next to this integration). Give the module a fixed IP address in your router. Never tested with a real module. Unofficial integration, not affiliated with nasWebio. |
| Address of the module | `string` | Yes | The IP address of the module (the one of its web page), optionally with its HTTPS port (443 by default). |
| Login of the module | `string` | Yes | The login of the web page of the module. |
| Password of the module | `secret` | Yes | Kept by Gladys in its database, never shown again, sent only to the module (as the module expects it, a SHA-1 hash, over the HTTPS connection whose certificate is pinned). |
| How the states arrive | `section` | No | The module sends its states to http:\/\/\<address of Gladys>:\{\{port:nasweb_push\}\}/ (port chosen by Gladys; \{\{gladys_host\}\} is how your browser reaches Gladys). The port exists once the address of the module, the login and the password are saved: save, then reload this screen. Type below the IP address of the Gladys machine as the module reaches it: the integration subscribes the module itself, with a secret address (sent in clear over HTTP by the module). Allow this port in the firewall of the Gladys machine if it has one. |
| Address of Gladys | `string` | No | The IP address of the machine running Gladys on your local network, without a port. |
| Check the sender of the states | `boolean` | No | Accept states only from the address of the module. Turn it off only if the status says the states come from another address because Docker hides the real one on this machine: then anyone who has read the secret address can post forged states, and so start your scenes. |
| Relay outputs | `section` | No | A relay may drive a lamp, but also a pump, a boiler, a heater or a gate. A switch is reached by "turn everything off" of voice assistants and scenes: so only the outputs you declare safe become switches; the others stay read only. Commands stay off until you allow them. |
| Outputs declared safe | `string` | No | The numbers of the outputs (parameter NASWEB_OUTPUT in the Discovery tab), separated by commas. Only loads that may be switched off or on at any time (a lamp, a socket for a lamp). |
| Allow the commands | `boolean` | No | Off: the outputs declared safe are shown as switches but every command is refused. |
| Language of the messages | `select` | No |  |

## How to install NASweb in Gladys

1. In Gladys, open **Integrations**: NASweb appears in the catalog, next to the native integrations, with a community badge.
2. Click **Install**. Gladys pulls the Docker image (`ghcr.io/lm1lc3n7/gladys-nasweb:0.1.1`), starts it in a sandbox isolated from the core, and generates the integration's interface (devices, discovery and configuration).
3. Open the **Configuration** screen of the integration, fill in the settings, and save.
4. You can also install it directly from its repository URL: [https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-nasweb](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-nasweb).

NASweb requires Gladys `>=5.1.0`. The catalog inside Gladys refreshes every hour, so a new version becomes available at most one hour after its release.

Not running Gladys yet? It is free and open source: [follow the installation guide](/docs/) to get started.

## About external integrations

NASweb is an **external integration**: a community integration packaged as a Docker container and published on GitHub, that Gladys installs in one click and runs in a sandbox isolated from its core. It is published and maintained by [LM1LC3N7](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7), not by the Gladys core team.
